analysis.one_liner: Requires crypto exchanges holding customer assets to disclose proof of reserves to the SEC.
analysis.headline: The bill died in committee without a single cosponsor or a vote before the 117th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require cryptocurrency exchanges that hold customer assets to regularly tell the Securities and Exchange Commission how many assets they hold compared with what they owe customers. The point is to make sure an exchange actually has the customer money it claims to have, the kind of check that was missing when the FTX exchange collapsed in late 2022.
analysis.who_benefits: People who keep money or crypto on an exchange. If an exchange holds assets for customers, it would have to show the SEC that its holdings match its debts to customers, so customers could learn sooner if an exchange was short on funds or lending out customer money. Regulators would also get a steady stream of balance-sheet data instead of finding out after a collapse.

how_it_helps.text: Requires any cryptocurrency exchange that holds assets on behalf of customers to periodically disclose proof of reserves to the SEC, including the amount of assets held compared to the exchange's liabilities [S2][S3].

This addresses the situation revealed by the FTX collapse, where an exchange used or lost customer funds and customers could not see the gap until it was too late; the bill's disclosures are designed to surface that mismatch to a regulator on a recurring schedule [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Crypto exchanges bear the cost of preparing and filing recurring reserve disclosures, and they lose the ability to keep their balance sheets private. Smaller exchanges would feel compliance costs more than large ones.

drawbacks.text: Disclosure to the SEC does not by itself prevent an exchange from becoming insolvent or misusing funds; it only gives the regulator information, and the bill leaves the frequency and form of disclosure to the SEC to define [S3].

The bill covers only exchanges that hold assets for customers, so trading platforms that do not take custody of customer assets, and other corners of the crypto market, would face no comparable disclosure requirement [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real but narrow: it gives the SEC a running check on whether exchanges hold what they owe customers, which is precisely the check that was absent before the FTX collapse. The costs are compliance burdens on exchanges and the fact that transparency with a regulator does not guarantee protection — the SEC would still have to act on what it learns. On balance a modest, targeted safeguard rather than a sweeping fix for crypto risk.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in early December 2022 and referred to the House Financial Services Committee, which never acted on it before the Congress ended in early January 2023.

narrative.text: Rep. Ritchie Torres (D-NY) introduced the Crypto Exchange Disclosure Act on December 2, 2022 [S1][S5].
The same day, the bill was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services, and no further action was taken on it [S5].
No other member signed on as a cosponsor [S4].
The 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023, and the bill died in committee without a markup, a floor vote, or any action in the Senate [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Cryptocurrency exchanges are better off: they never had to file proof-of-reserves disclosures with the SEC, and their balance sheets remain private. Exchange customers gained no new protection against an exchange that does not actually hold the assets it claims to hold.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Crypto exchanges, which face no reserve disclosure

for.name: Rep. Ritchie Torres
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill, which would require exchanges holding customer assets to disclose reserves to the SEC

against.name: House Financial Services Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on December 2, 2022 and took no further action on the bill before the Congress ended

sides.party_line_note: The bill never reached a vote, so no one is on record for or against it; it was sponsored by one Democrat and drew no cosponsors of either party.

industries.note: The bill would require exchanges that hold customer assets to prove to the SEC that their holdings match their liabilities, ending the practice of keeping balance sheets private. Solvent exchanges would also gain credibility with customers and regulators, so the interest is not uniformly opposed to transparency.
